endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Verify information sharing and feedback mechanisms among individuals and organizations regarding any negative impact from GAI systems.

endorsements.title: Perspective on patient and non-academic partner engagement for the responsible integration of large language models in health chatbots
endorsements.quote: To support meaningful and sustained collaboration with patients and non-academic partners, especially when sensitive or distressing topics may arise, projects must allocate dedicated financial resources and assign clear managerial responsibility (e.g., an engagement coordinator or patient-partnership lead) to oversee communication, ethics, and continuity of participation.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether dedicated time and funding for outreach, feedback, and recourse processes improve how generative AI systems perform or how patients fare. The recommendation rests on one federal framework and one commentary, so health systems adopting it would be acting on expert judgment rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Both endorsements are a framework and a commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and any expected benefit remains a hypothesis.

NIST AI 600-1 says organizations should verify feedback and information-sharing mechanisms about negative impacts from generative AI. This language is voluntary guidance, and nothing supplied here ties it to an FDA, ONC, or state statutory requirement. Systems may cite it as a reference standard, but it does not set a funding level.

The commentary calls for dedicated money and a named coordinator so that patient partners can take part in chatbot projects, including when distressing topics arise. The source reflects a stated patient-engagement priority. No data show whether funded recourse channels help patients reach a human or correct AI errors faster.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether allocating staff time or budget to feedback and recourse processes changes the volume of reported generative AI problems, the speed of their resolution, patient trust, or harm rates. Evaluations comparing funded engagement structures with ad hoc processes, and reporting the cost per resolved issue, would give administrators a basis for sizing these investments.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. These groups may face greater barriers to using feedback and recourse channels, and whether dedicated resources reduce those barriers is unknown.
